dataset.name: CMU Keystroke Dynamics Benchmark (Killourhy & Maxion 2009)
dataset.size: 20,400 samples, 51 typists x 400 repetitions of one password

notes: The adversaries are synthetic. They bound the rules; they are not evidence about real attackers.
One practised password, typed 400 times by each of 51 people.

Humans and bots were recorded on different machines and screen sizes; check shortcutRisk before trusting any AUC. A feature that separates only because of the sample clock tells you about the recorder, not the visitor.
Balabit sessions are remote-desktop work, not a web task, so its pointer timing includes network jitter; it is used for the human-side rates only.
Reaction times here come from a keyboard task; the product asks for a click or tap, which adds pointing time. Treat the window result as a LOWER bound on human lateness.
The Stroop task in this dataset has more than two colours; an error is mapped to "chose the word" for the two-colour product, which can only make humans look worse, never better.
A UA string is a claim, not evidence. This measures only how well CaptchaMe recognises what a client SAYS it is. A bot that says "Chrome" is invisible here.
Agents that run in a person's own Chrome (Atlas, Comet, Claude in Chrome) are indistinguishable from that person at the HTTP level (stated by mintlify/agent-traffic itself).

limits: GitHub-hosted data only. Eight datasets that matter most are blocked-here; their entries list what to allow.
Humans and bots in delbot were recorded on different machines. AUCs there carry a shortcut risk; the harness prints it.
Adversaries in the typing test are synthetic and mine; they bound the rules, they are not evidence about real attackers.
CMU is one practised password and the Stroop data is keyboard-based. Both are favourable to the rules.
Nothing here tests ring, pulse, reflex, targets, beat or voice on people. Their thresholds are still unvalidated.
